title: Benedict: pray and work
hookLine: the Rule of Benedict balances prayer, work and rest in community (Rule 48)

cards: Two lists sit on a kitchen table. One says church, prayer, the quiet ten minutes if there's time. The other says emails, laundry, the commute, the spreadsheet, the dishes.

The first list looks like the spiritual part of life. The second takes up almost all the hours. A monk in Italy wrote a little rulebook for his community, and it quietly tears up the line between those two lists.
Prayer has its hours. Work has its hours. Both belong to God.
The well-known summary of his Rule: ora et labora.

teach.b: Benedict of Nursia lived as the old Roman world in the west was coming apart. Tradition says he first lived alone in a cave, then gathered monks together, and founded a monastery at Monte Cassino.
For them he wrote the Rule of Saint Benedict, seventy-three short chapters on how to live together. Its very first word is listen.
The Rule sets the day by the bells: prayer together, seven times in the day and once in the night. In between, work, in the fields, the kitchen, the workshop, and slow reading of scripture.

teach.h: IDLENESS IS THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.
teach.b: Chapter forty-eight begins with a line in Latin that monks have quoted ever since: otiositas inimica est animae, idleness is the enemy of the soul. Then it lays out the hours for work and for reading, season by season.

teach.h: THE MOTTO ISN'T IN THE RULE.
teach.b: The words ora et labora, pray and work, are not actually in the Rule. They're a later motto, a fair summary of it. And the Rule goes further than balance.
Benedict tells the monk who looks after the kitchen and storeroom to treat every tool and pot of the monastery as if it were a sacred vessel of the altar.
The bread knife and the chalice, handled with the same care. Not prayer, and then the real stuff. Work done as prayer.
Monks and nuns have lived by this Rule ever since, and some people outside monasteries, Catholic, Anglican and others, use it as a guide for ordinary life.
This week went from the house on the rock to the desert and the cell. Benedict brings the desert indoors, into a kitchen.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, praying together at set hours and working in between, and lay Christians called oblates follow the Rule in their own homes and jobs.

games.q: you're the monk in charge of the monastery kitchen. how does the Rule tell you to treat the pots and tools?
o: as if they were sacred vessels of the altar.
as cheap things that don't matter.
hand them to someone else to clean.
games.why: the bread knife and the chalice, handled with the same care. that's pray and work.

practice: In Benedict's house, when the signal for prayer sounded, the Rule told the monks to put down whatever was in their hands and go.
Choose one moment in today's work, an alarm, the top of the hour, the kettle boiling, and picture yourself stopping there for one minute, hands still.
If you pray, that minute can be prayer; if not, let it be a breath between tasks.

wordCard.voice: Benedict, the monk who wrote the Rule that set prayer and work side by side. Ora et labora, pray and work, is a later motto, but a fair summary of his Rule.

orig.note: Latin: pray and work; a later motto summing up Benedict's Rule.
